macro.overview: The FOMC kept rates at 3.50-3.75% on 07-29 in a 9-3 vote, with Hammack, Kashkari and Logan favouring a 25 bp hike. The next day brought slower growth than the Q1 pace alongside firm year-on-year inflation. [Probable] Equities fell on the decision day and recovered over the next two sessions.

anchor.question: Does slower growth, with core inflation still at 3.3%, change the policy path signalled by the July dissents? [Speculative]
paragraphs: The dissents favoured higher rates, while the Q2 real GDP advance estimate of +1.5% annualized on 07-30 was below Q1’s +2.1% pace. These releases leave growth and inflation pulling the policy discussion in different directions. [Probable]

Rate-path expectations can transmit into the valuations of long-duration equities in this portfolio: TSMC, Microsoft, Alphabet, QQQ and VOO. [Probable] BOXX has short-duration exposure, so the channel differs from that of the equity positions. [Probable]

June PCE was -0.1% m/m and +3.7% y/y; core PCE was +0.1% m/m and +3.3% y/y. The modest monthly core reading is a counterweight to the firm annual reading, rather than a settled policy outcome. [Probable]

The remaining uncertainty is whether slower activity and persistent annual inflation continue together. [Speculative] The July Employment Situation on 08-07 is an observable for payrolls and wages alongside this growth-and-inflation tension. [Probable]

If the employment release points to softer activity, watch how rate-path expectations and these equity exposures respond; if wage pressure persists, watch whether the case reflected in the July dissents remains in focus. [Speculative] These are conditional observation paths. [Speculative]

analysisItems.heading: TSMC — 21.7% of the portfolio, the single largest position
paragraphs: TSMC is the largest position at 21.7%, above the 20% single-stock high-concentration threshold. Its +7.64% rise on 07-30 occurred after Microsoft's earnings release; the timing alone does not establish new orders or a TSMC-specific catalyst.

The company-specific background predates this window: on 07-16, TSMC attributed Q2 performance to demand for leading-edge processes, which accounted for 77% of wafer revenue at 7nm and below. [Established] The documented business channel is demand for those processes reaching TSMC through wafer production; Microsoft's cloud growth does not quantify its share of that demand. [Probable]

Expansion also has a cash and margin dimension. The earlier Q2 disclosures show operating cash generation alongside factory investment, while management's Q3 gross-margin guidance of 65-67% is below Q2's 67.7%, despite higher revenue guidance. [Established] More sales therefore do not establish a uniform improvement in production economics. [Probable] Next observables are the revenue mix, factory spending and gross margin in subsequent disclosures; the guidance is not an achieved result.

analysisItems.heading: Microsoft — 8.3% of the portfolio
paragraphs: Microsoft's 8.3% position rose +15.51% on 07-30 after its 07-29 fiscal Q4 release. Revenue was $90.01B; Azure and other cloud services grew 43% year on year. [Established] This is a documented operating development alongside the price move, rather than an explanation inferred from the price chart.

The business channel is cloud-service demand reaching Microsoft's revenue: Microsoft Cloud generated $59.3B, up 27% year on year. Commercial remaining performance obligations of $678B describe contracted revenue still to be recognized, not revenue already earned this quarter. audience.heading: For investors who stay through the cycle
paragraphs: Portfonia is a software tool for investors who stay through the cycle. A deep reading of trends, cycles, and fundamentals takes time, and it needs information closely tied to what you hold, delivered continuously and reliably.

Our work is to take what is scattered across news, macro events, and company developments, and map it back, systematically, onto every position you hold. That is how you get depth and breadth that actually fit the names you follow — so you can see where an asset sits, what is changing around it, and which signals are worth a closer look. Judgment stays yours. We make sure that judgment sits on solid information.
Market cycles rise and fall. Portfonia keeps the information flowing through every one of them.

sections.heading: 1. Overview

sections.heading: 2. Information We Collect
body: Account information: your email address and authentication credentials, handled by our authentication provider.
Holdings and investment data: positions, brokers/custodians, and quantities you upload, plus any investment-style questionnaire responses you provide.
Usage information: basic session and activity data needed to operate the Service securely (for example, sign-in timestamps and idle-timeout enforcement).

Payment and credit information: purchases are processed by {merchantOfRecord} as Merchant of Record. {merchantOfRecord} collects your payment details and billing information under its own privacy notice; we receive transaction records such as order ID, amount, currency, country, and the email used at checkout, but never your full card number. body: We use your data solely to generate and deliver your portfolio reports and to operate, secure, and improve the Service. We do not sell your data, and we do not use your holdings to build or improve any third-party product.
We use payment and credit records to provide your plan, process refunds, and meet accounting and tax obligations.

sections.heading: 4. Data Storage and Security
body: Your holdings are encrypted at rest with field-level encryption, and so is the data derived from them: report text and the inputs each report is built from, daily portfolio snapshots, parsed uploads, holding change history and report coverage notes. The encryption key is not stored in the database or in its backups. Access to production systems is restricted, administrative actions are logged, and our administrative tools do not display your holdings or reports.
No system is perfectly secure, and we cannot guarantee absolute security, but protecting your data is treated as a first-class engineering requirement, not an afterthought.

sections.heading: 5. Third-Party Processing
body: Generating a report involves sending portions of your data to third-party large-language-model providers to compose the report text. By default, every such call is configured to opt out of the provider using your data for model training.
Payments are processed by {merchantOfRecord}, which acts as Merchant of Record and handles your payment information under its own privacy notice.

Holding change history from web, file upload, Agent writes and rollbacks is stored encrypted for 30 days. You can view it on the web; your Agent can read it while Jade is active. agent.limits: Limits combine all your tokens. Single-row holdings POST/PUT/PATCH/DELETE share 30 requests per minute and 100 per hour; request 31 in one minute locks all Agent access for 15 minutes. Other calls, including GET, whole PUT and validate, allow 20 per endpoint per hour and 10 across endpoints per minute; request 11 locks access for 15 minutes. A refusal returns Retry-After.
agent.quiet: Requests pause from five minutes before a heavy scheduled job’s scheduled time until five minutes after it finishes, including intelligence collection and scheduled briefings.
agent.notice: Successful reads of current holdings, holding change history, snapshots and Jade risk results share one access notice per Eastern Time day. Every successful Agent write request, including unchanged writes, may trigger a separate daily modification notice. Validation and idempotent replay send no data notice. The link revokes every API token on the account at once, including tokens used by other agents. Create new tokens afterwards for agents you still want to run. Revocation does not undo saved changes. An Agent write or file upload that sharply reduces holdings rows or changes total value may trigger a separate alert email, at most one per Eastern Time date of the write.
agent.tokenRule: You can have up to 5 active tokens. Tokens unused for 60 days expire automatically.
agent.permissionNote: Permission is fixed at creation. To change it, create a new token and revoke the old one. Current-holdings reads, validation and change history require active Jade; changes also require holdings write.

docs.endpointsLead: Detailed fields and calling conventions for each endpoint are in llms.txt and agent.md. The following is a summary of each endpoint.
docs.reportsAccess: Applies to any active plan. Read-only tokens and holdings-write tokens are both accepted.
docs.reportsAction: Read the body of briefings that have already been generated.
docs.reportsNote: Give a start date and an end date, including both days, in Eastern Time. At most the five newest briefings in that range are returned. To read older briefings, move the end date earlier.
docs.snapshotsAccess: Applies during an active Advanced or Jade period. Read-only tokens and holdings-write tokens are both accepted.
docs.snapshotsNote: Give a start date and an end date, including both days, in Eastern Time. One request covers at most 30 days. After a successful read, at most one access notice is sent that day.
docs.intelAccess: Available with active Advanced or Jade, using either token permission. Advanced receives headlines only; Jade also receives headline summaries and included article text for holdings and macro themes.
docs.intelAction: Read intelligence related to your holdings.
docs.intelNote: Choose an Eastern Time date within the last 7 days, including today, or an offset timestamp in since mode within the same range. Since mode returns at most 24 hours of newly ingested material, ending 5 minutes before now; store next_since and repeat while has_more. Both tiers include macro headlines for the latest briefing’s themes. Source links are not included.
docs.holdingsReadAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Read-only tokens and holdings-write tokens are both accepted.
docs.holdingsReadAction: Read the current holdings book as saved.
docs.holdingsReadNote: Cash and watched holdings are included. The same instrument kept in different accounts is stored separately. Successful reads of current holdings, holding change history, snapshots and Jade risk results share at most one access notice per Eastern Time day.
docs.holdingsReplaceAllAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Only a holdings-write token is accepted.
docs.holdingsReplaceAllAction: Submit the whole current holdings book.
docs.holdingsReplaceAllNote: Every existing holding must be listed, kept or explicitly deleted. An omitted row is not deleted, and that submission is rejected. At least one holding must remain. A new holding carries no existing id. Submission order is the saved order. Jade allows at most 100 rows, and cash and watched holdings count. After success the version increases by one, and one modification notice may be sent that day.
docs.holdingsAddAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Only a holdings-write token is accepted.
docs.holdingsAddAction: Add one holding at the end of the current book.
docs.holdingsAddNote: A request key is required. Within 24 hours, the same key and the same content return the first result and do not add another row. The same key with different content is rejected. The row caps are the same as for the whole-book update. After success the version increases by one, and one modification notice may be sent that day.
docs.holdingsReplaceAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Only a holdings-write token is accepted.
docs.holdingsReplaceAction: Replace the writable fields of this one holding.
docs.holdingsReplaceNote: Omitted optional fields are cleared. Name, currency, and pricing mode must be submitted. This holding keeps its position. Send the version just read. If the version has changed, read again and then submit. After success the version increases by one, and one modification notice may be sent that day.
docs.holdingsPatchHeading: Change some fields of one holding
docs.holdingsPatchAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Only a holdings-write token is accepted.
docs.holdingsPatchNote: Fields that were not submitted stay as stored. A field is cleared only when it is explicitly submitted as empty. Required fields cannot be cleared. A successful request increases the version by one even when the stored content is unchanged. If the version does not match, read again and then change it. One modification notice may be sent that day.
docs.holdingsDeleteAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Only a holdings-write token is accepted.
docs.holdingsDeleteNote: The last holding cannot be deleted. To clear the whole book, use the web page. Send the current version. After success the version increases by one, and one modification notice may be sent that day.
docs.holdingsValidateHeading: Validate a holdings change before writing
docs.holdingsValidateAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Read-only tokens and holdings-write tokens are both accepted.
docs.holdingsValidateAction: Validate whether a whole-book update, an addition, a single-holding replacement, or a partial change would be accepted.
docs.holdingsValidateNote: Nothing is saved, no prices are fetched, no holdings notice is sent, and the version is not reserved. A passing validation does not mean a later write will succeed.
docs.endpointsClosing: These endpoints do not connect to a broker and do not submit trades. Every request leaves an audit record. The audit does not store the holdings body or the full token.
docs.tokenAccess: Available on every plan, including without an active subscription. Read-only tokens and holdings-write tokens are both accepted.
docs.tokenAction: Lets your agent check what this token may do before it starts: the token's name, prefix, permission, creation and expiry times, and which capabilities your current plan allows right now.
docs.tokenNote: Capabilities follow your plan at the time of the call, so an agent can call this first and stop instead of failing later. Uses the normal read limits and quiet windows. Sends no access notice.
docs.changesAccess: Applies during an active Jade period. Read-only tokens and holdings-write tokens are both accepted.
docs.changesAction: Read field-level before and after values from web, file upload and Agent writes.
docs.changesNote: Give inclusive Eastern Time dates within the last 30 days. At most the 100 newest groups are returned; narrow the range when truncated. History is encrypted and kept for 30 days. Reads share one daily access notice with current holdings, snapshots and Jade risk results.
docs.jadeAccess: Active Jade; read-only and holdings-write tokens
docs.jadeAction: Read the results of your five Jade risk tools, including every series.
docs.jadeNote: Tools: replay, tail-risk, stress, style and tracking. Stress requires one scenario per request. Together these routes allow one request per 3 minutes and at most 10 per hour per user, in addition to the existing Agent limits and quiet windows.

tailRisk.title: Tail risk (VaR / CVaR)
tailRisk.intro: VaR (Value at Risk) is the loss line that most days or months in the replay stayed within at the chosen confidence level; it is not the largest possible loss. CVaR (Conditional Value at Risk, also called Expected Shortfall) is the average loss on the days or months beyond that line. Both come from the five-year replay of the holdings you have today.
tailRisk.noQuestionnaire: Complete the investment questionnaire to show the reference line.
tailRisk.insufficient99: 99% needs at least 500 daily returns; this replay has {count}.
tailRisk.proxyUnderstates: Holdings represented by an index ETF lose their own swings, so VaR and CVaR may understate tail losses.
tailRisk.window: Five-year replay {start} to {end}: {count} daily returns, and {windows} overlapping 21-trading-day windows (about {independent} non-overlapping).
tailRisk.methodText: Historical simulation. With n returns at confidence c, the tail holds k = n × (1 − c) observations, rounded up. VaR is the k-th worst loss and CVaR is the average of the k worst. One-month figures use actual 21-trading-day returns from overlapping windows, not a one-day figure scaled up, so neighbouring windows share most of their days. Amounts apply the percentages to the current value of the holdings included in the replay, in {currency}.
tailRisk.normalLine: If returns followed a normal distribution with the replay's own mean and volatility, {level}% VaR would be {dayVar} (1 day) and {monthVar} (1 month), and CVaR {dayCvar} and {monthCvar}. The gap from the figures above shows how far the replay's tails differ from a normal distribution.
tailRisk.referenceText: The reference line takes the volatility level that the Overview Risk indicator treats as beyond your questionnaire answers (risk appetite, horizon and objective) and converts it into a loss at this confidence level, assuming a normal distribution with zero mean. It is a point of comparison, not a judgement, and it is not a normal-distribution version of your VaR: the VaR above uses the replay's actual distribution.
tailRisk.limitations: The figures reflect only what happened inside the five-year replay; events outside it are not included. The replay uses the holdings you have today, so hindsight applies. This describes the past and is not a forecast.
tailRisk.loadError: Tail risk could not be loaded. Try again later.
tailRisk.whatItSays: How to read it: at 95%, a one-day VaR of 2.0% means that on about 95 of every 100 days in the replay the portfolio lost less than 2.0%. On the other 5 days it lost more, and CVaR is their average loss. The one-month column does the same for periods of 21 trading days. The benchmark rows show the same figures for the selected index, so you can see whether your holdings' bad days were deeper or shallower.
tailRisk.readChart: The chart counts how many days fell into each band of daily return, losses on the left. The marked lines are the one-day VaR, CVaR and, if you completed the questionnaire, the reference line. A long, thin left tail means rare but deep losses.

stress.whatItSays: How to read it: "Peak to trough" is how much this portfolio would have gained or lost between the S&P 500's high and its low in that episode. "Largest drawdown in the window" is the deepest fall of the portfolio itself inside the window, which can happen on different dates. The chart runs from six months before the peak to six months after the trough, with 0% at the peak.
stress.readBars: Each bar is one asset class's share of the peak-to-trough return. A bar to the left of the center line pulled the portfolio down; to the right, it added to it. A bar's size reflects both how much that asset class moved and how much of the portfolio it was, so a small holding that fell sharply can still have a short bar. Bar lengths are relative to the largest bar. The figures add up to the portfolio's peak-to-trough return, up to rounding.

style.title: Style exposure
style.intro: Breaks the last three months of your portfolio's movement into a mix of recognizable styles and asset classes, and shows how much of that movement the mix does not explain.
style.lowFit: R² is {r2}, below 0.60: these styles explain little of this portfolio's movement, so the mix describes it only loosely.
style.sampleNote: Based on about three months of data ({count} overlapping three-day returns); a single market event can dominate the result.
style.proxyFit: Some holdings follow index ETFs as proxies. Those ETFs resemble the styles above, so they raise the fit mechanically.
style.insufficient: Fewer than {min} three-day returns are available ({count}), so no style mix is shown.
style.methodText: Prices are total return (dividends reinvested), converted to {currency} at each day's exchange rate. Each sample is the return over three trading days, computed every day, so neighbouring samples overlap; this lines up markets that close at different times. The weights make the mix's returns as close as possible to the portfolio's returns (least squares), with every weight at least zero and the weights summing to one (Sharpe's returns-based style analysis). R² is one minus the variance of the unexplained part divided by the variance of the portfolio's returns; it can be below zero when no mix follows the portfolio. Unexplained volatility is the standard deviation of the unexplained part, scaled by √(252/3).
style.limitations: Style weights are a statistical equivalent, not the holdings themselves. The window is fixed at three months and does not follow the replay span; it describes the past, not the future. Overlapping samples are not independent, so the effective sample is smaller than the count shown.
style.loadError: Style exposure could not be loaded.
style.whatItSays: What it says: which mix of broad market styles would have moved most like your portfolio over the last three months. It is a statistical resemblance, not what you actually own. It helps you see whether holdings that look different were in fact moving to the same few styles.
style.readBars: Reading the bars: each bar is that style's weight in the mix. Weights are zero or more and add up to 100%. For example, "US large-cap growth 60%" means your portfolio's ups and downs looked most like a mix holding 60% in US large-cap growth stocks. A style is listed when your portfolio or the benchmark gives it a weight above 0%, so a row can show 0% in one column. The benchmark column shows the same breakdown for the selected index. R² (R-squared) is the share of your portfolio's movement that the mix explains: 1.00 is all of it, 0.50 is half. Unexplained volatility is the size of the remaining movement on a yearly scale, which comes from what is specific to your holdings. REITs (real estate investment trusts) are listed companies that own income-producing property.

tracking.teInsufficient: Tracking error needs at least {min} five-day returns; this span has {count}.
tracking.proxyNote: Some holdings follow index ETFs as proxies. Those ETFs move like index-based references, so tracking error may be understated.
tracking.referencePending: Price history for the reference is being prepared. It is updated once a day after the US market close.
tracking.referenceUnavailable: The reference cannot be computed for this span because one of its components has no prices for part of it.
tracking.methodText: Prices are total return (dividends reinvested), converted to {currency} at each day's exchange rate; the cash component stays constant in {currency}. The reference is rebalanced to its weights every day, so its daily return is the weighted sum of its components' daily returns. Excess return is your portfolio's cumulative return minus the reference's; annualized excess is the difference between the two annualized returns. Tracking error is the standard deviation of the difference between the two five-day returns, computed every day and scaled by √(252/5). Five-day returns line up markets that close at different times; daily returns would add differences that come only from the closing times.
tracking.limitations: You choose the reference; the results describe the difference from it, not whether it suits you. Overlapping five-day samples are not independent, so the effective sample is smaller than the count shown, especially for short spans. Your portfolio is today's holdings replayed without rebalancing, while the reference is rebalanced daily. This describes the past and is not a forecast.
tracking.whatItSays: What it says: how differently your holdings moved from a reference portfolio you define, such as 60% US stocks and 40% US bonds. Excess return is the gap in total return between the two; the chart shows how that gap built up, above zero when your portfolio was ahead and below zero when it was behind. Tracking error measures how unevenly the gap moved, whichever side ended ahead: low means your portfolio moved closely with the reference, high means it often moved differently. As a rough guide, 5% means the yearly gap typically varied by about 5 percentage points. REITs (real estate investment trusts) are listed companies that own income-producing property.

whatIf.title: Holdings rebalancing what-if: reading the comparison
whatIf.intro: A historical calculation of current holdings and up to two user-edited versions, with separate rebalancing rules.
whatIf.chartCaption: {portfolio}. {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Cumulative returns under no rebalancing, monthly and quarterly rules; the shared starting mixture and dates are the same for all three lines.

s1.heading: What the page answers
s1.p1: Holdings rebalancing what-if compares the holdings recorded today with up to two versions of amounts and rebalancing rules chosen by you. It applies past prices to those inputs. The question is how those specified mixtures trace different paths over the same history, with the calculation and its data limits visible beside the results.
s1.p2: This is a historical calculation, not a forecast or an assessment of any version. It does not describe the transactions that actually occurred in your account. A version can contain amounts or instruments that were never part of your account during the selected dates. The column order is fixed; neither order nor colour assigns a ranking.

s2.heading: The three columns
s2.p1: Current is fixed and matches the Jade replay, tail-risk and historical-stress cards for the same currency and replay span. Version A and Version B begin as independent copies. Edit each row’s amount in the display currency; its share updates with the version’s total. A zero amount omits that row from the calculation. An empty amount counts as zero, commas used as thousands separators are ignored, and digits beyond two decimal places are dropped. The footer shows the total, its ratio to the current total and the signed difference, so a change in portfolio size is visible alongside a change in composition.
s2.p2: The additional ETF list is fixed: SPY, QQQ, EFA, EEM, 2800.HK, 510300.SS, ISF.L, EXSA.DE, 1306.T, 069500.KS, AGG and GLD. Cash is another available row. Added cash is denominated in the display currency, with the entered amount as its current base-currency value. It enters the calculation as cash rather than an ETF price series; there is no modelled interest return for that same-currency cash row.
s2.p3: The confirmation dialog appears only when a version’s displayed ratio falls outside the inclusive band from ninety-nine percent to one hundred and one percent of the current total. That displayed ratio is rounded half-up to a decimal place before the band is checked. The dialog identifies the affected versions and their ratios; Confirm calculates with those amounts, while Cancel returns to editing.
s2.p4: Changing the replay span does not calculate. Changing currency reloads current amounts and resets both versions to copies, without calculating. Calculate submits both versions; earlier results retain the span and currency used for that calculation until another submission succeeds. Each user can submit once every two minutes; an early attempt shows a countdown. Inputs remain for another editing round but nothing is saved after the page reloads. With no valued current holdings, the page links to holdings instead of showing the editor.

s3.heading: Three calendar rules
s3.p1: No rebalancing leaves quantities unchanged as prices move. Monthly and quarterly calculations start at the version’s own weights and reset to them at the close of the first valid trading day of each new calendar month or quarter. They use the closing portfolio value at that reset, with no external cash flow.
s3.p2: In the committed example window, the monthly line resets {monthlyResets} times and the quarterly line resets {quarterlyResets} times. Every reset uses the initial {spyStart} SPY and {aggStart} AGG weights. The value for the reset day is calculated first, and the new quantities apply to subsequent price changes. A calendar boundary during a market closure therefore uses the first valid trading day, rather than a fabricated price on the calendar date.
s3.p3: The no-rebalancing line begins at those same {spyStart} SPY and {aggStart} AGG weights. By {end}, its value weights are {endSpyWeight} SPY and {endAggWeight} AGG. The quantities have not changed; the two price paths have changed their shares of the total. This drift is what a reset removes at each scheduled close. Between resets, the monthly and quarterly mixtures also drift.

s4.heading: Where each path starts
s4.p1: On the Jade page, replay and tail risk without rebalancing carry today’s quantities back through history. Rebalanced columns instead begin at today’s weights on the window’s first day. These are different starting conventions: a current value weight does not imply that the same weight applied on every earlier date. The tail-risk calculation uses its fixed historical replay window, while the chart follows the span selected for Calculate.
s4.p2: Stress scenarios begin every column at today’s weights on the scenario’s first valid day, as the existing Jade stress tool does. Without rebalancing the weights then drift; monthly and quarterly columns reset on their calendar boundaries after the reset day’s close. Stress therefore has the same starting convention across columns even though their subsequent rules differ. The selected replay span does not change those scenario windows.

s5.heading: The example: three lines
s5.p1: This public example uses {portfolio}, starting on {start} and ending on {end}. All three lines begin with the same mixture at the first date: no rebalancing, monthly and quarterly. They use the committed SPY and AGG adjusted closing prices, including distributions. This is a fixed illustration, separate from any person’s holdings.
s5.p2: The common starting mixture isolates the effect of the calendar rule within this example. It differs from the no-rebalancing replay on the Jade page, which carries today’s quantities backward. The chart places cumulative returns on the same date axis; the table applies the same metric definitions and observation window to all three lines.
s5.p3: Cumulative return compares the final value with the initial value for the entire window. It is {none_cumulative} without rebalancing, {monthly_cumulative} with monthly resets and {quarterly_cumulative} with quarterly resets. These are changes in the example’s calculated value, including the adjusted-price distribution treatment. They are not the realized returns of a user’s account and do not assign a preference to a rule.
s5.p4: Annualized return expresses the full-window compounded change as a yearly rate using the elapsed calendar time. The values are {none_annualized} without rebalancing, {monthly_annualized} monthly and {quarterly_annualized} quarterly. This puts the total change on a common yearly scale; it does not mean that the path delivered that rate in each calendar year.
s5.p5: Annualized volatility describes the dispersion of consecutive daily returns, using their sample standard deviation scaled to a year. It is {none_volatility} without rebalancing, {monthly_volatility} monthly and {quarterly_volatility} quarterly. It concerns variation along each path, rather than the direction or size of its final cumulative return. The three figures use the same price dates.
s5.p6: Maximum drawdown is the largest decline from an earlier calculated peak to a subsequent trough in the window. It is {none_drawdown} without rebalancing, {monthly_drawdown} monthly and {quarterly_drawdown} quarterly. These negative figures describe a peak-to-trough interval within each path, not the full-window return. The number summarizes one observed decline and is not a boundary on future losses.

s6.heading: What the results show on the page
s6.p1: The Jade page displays a replay curve and its metrics for each column, then VaR and CVaR in percentage and currency amounts for daily and monthly horizons. VaR describes a historical loss boundary at the displayed confidence level; CVaR describes the average within the associated tail. They summarize the replay observations used for that column rather than a forecast of a particular future day or month.
s6.p2: The stress table places the five historical scenarios in time order. Each column reports the scenario peak-to-trough return and amount, together with its in-window maximum drawdown. Read columns across the same dates and result type, including each column’s rule and data-coverage notice. A pending or insufficient-data state is not a zero return. The page has no benchmark line, contribution bars or ranking.

s7.heading: Hindsight and omitted costs
s7.p1: The inputs are selected today and evaluated against known history. Trying multiple versions against the same prices favours whichever happened to match that period; this supplies no ranking or forecast. Costs, taxes and transaction timing are not modelled. The past paths describe these assumptions over these dates only.
s7.p2: A reset in practice would involve transactions. Their execution prices, costs, taxes and timing are outside this calculation; the model resets at the selected day’s closing values without those effects. Applying a different mixture repeatedly to familiar history also leaves the same hindsight limitation in place. A displayed difference records the assumptions and price path, rather than an assessment of which version fits a person.

s8.heading: The watermark
s8.p1: The repeated text across the result tables and chart identifies a calculation based only on user-defined assumptions. It also appears in screenshots. The same sentence is available as ordinary text for assistive technology; it is not an assessment of any version.
s8.p2: The watermark accompanies the results alongside the notices on hindsight, starting conventions and omitted costs. It identifies what the calculation represents when the chart or a table is viewed separately from the editor. It does not turn an illustrative historical path into a forecast.

replay.title: Holdings replay: reading the path
replay.intro: The replay makes the method visible through a fixed example using real SPY and AGG history. The example portfolio illustrates the calculation only. {exampleLabel}.

s1.heading: What the replay answers
s1.p1: The replay starts with the holdings you have today and takes their quantities back through a chosen span of up to five years. It asks how that same collection would have moved as prices changed. This is a hypothetical path, not a record of your own past account results. Assets that entered your account later still appear throughout the replay wherever history or a disclosed substitute is available. Its starting point is the chosen window, rather than the date your account began.

s2.heading: A path through the example
s2.p1: The example uses real SPY and AGG history, with {spyStart} allocated to SPY and {aggStart} to AGG at the start. The quantities stay unchanged. SPY appears separately as the comparison line. Both curves measure the change from their starting value, so their heights can be compared without a difference in starting amounts. The vertical markers locate the example’s maximum-drawdown peak and trough. They mark a particular fall inside the window, which need not begin on the first day or end on the last.

s3.heading: What each metric means
s3.p1: Cumulative return is the total change from the first value to the last. Here it is {cumulative}, compared with {spyCumulative} for SPY. It combines the whole path into one endpoint comparison; it does not describe how steady or uneven that path was.
s3.p2: Annualized return translates that endpoint change into a constant yearly rate over the actual calendar days. The example’s rate is {annualized}, and SPY’s is {spyAnnualized}. It is a conversion of historical results, not a rate promised for another year.
s3.p3: Annualized volatility describes how widely the daily returns varied, expressed on a yearly scale. It is {volatility} for the example and {spyVolatility} for SPY. It counts variation in both directions, so it differs from a measure of losses alone.
s3.p4: Maximum drawdown measures the deepest fall from a high to a later low, not the loss from the starting point. The example fell {drawdown} from {peak} to {trough}. SPY’s maximum drawdown was {spyDrawdown}, with its own peak and trough dates shown in the table.
s3.p5: Worst day identifies the most negative daily return. The example’s was {worstDay} on {worstDate}; SPY’s was {spyWorstDay} on that same date. This is a single observed day, rather than an estimate of the largest possible future loss.
s3.p6: Worst month compares calendar month-end values, using the first value as the first month’s base. The example’s worst calendar month was {worstMonthLabel}, at {worstMonth}; SPY returned {spyWorstMonth} that month. A calendar month differs from a rolling trading-day window.

s4.heading: Unchanged quantities, changing weights
s4.p1: No rebalancing means the number of units stays the same while each asset’s share of the value changes. In this example, SPY starts at {spyStart} and ends at {endSpyWeight}. The final mix therefore differs from the starting mix even though neither quantity changed. The replay does not model your own trades, additions or withdrawals. A portfolio repeatedly reset to its initial weights would trace a different path, because the quantities would change along the way.

s5.heading: Total return and distributions
s5.p1: Total return includes distributions as well as price changes. Dividends are treated as reinvested, rather than removed from the series as cash. The example uses adjusted closes. For funds, the tool uses net asset value (NAV), the value per fund unit, with distributions reinvested. That differs from a price-only chart: a distribution can lower the quoted price without representing the same loss in total value. The treatment describes the calculation, rather than your actual distribution choices.

s6.heading: Proxies and history before listing
s6.p1: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a fund listed on an exchange that tracks an index. A holding without its own usable history is represented by an index ETF chosen by market or asset class. Cash stays constant in its own currency. Before a later listing, the tool fills history with its market ETF, scaled by beta: a measure of how strongly the holding moved with that ETF. Beta is 1 when fewer than 60 samples are available. The card discloses each method and the approximated share, with an additional notice at 66%.

s7.heading: Why short spans magnify annualized figures
s7.p1: Annualization stretches a short observation into a yearly rate. From {monthStart} to {end}, the example returned {monthCumulative}; the same change annualizes to {monthAnnualized}. The larger yearly figure is a mathematical conversion, not additional observed growth. A short span contains fewer market episodes, and one event can occupy much of it. On a one-month span the card hides the worst-month metric, while retaining the other measures and the short-span explanation.

s8.heading: The hindsight in today’s holdings
s8.p1: Today’s holdings were often selected partly because of how they performed. Replaying them through earlier years therefore includes hindsight: the collection was known at the end, even if it was not known at the start. Assets no longer in your account are absent. The replay describes a past path for the current collection; it does not reconstruct every decision in your account or forecast what happens next.

s9.heading: Currency over time
s9.p1: The tool converts values to the display currency using each day’s historical exchange rate. An asset’s local-currency path and its display-currency path can differ because the exchange rate also changed. Cash can consequently vary in the display currency while remaining constant in its own currency. The table and chart use the same currency basis throughout, keeping the portfolio and comparison series on a consistent basis.

s10.heading: References
s10.p1: Jorion, P., Value at Risk: The New Benchmark for Managing Financial Risk, historical simulation chapter.

var.title: Tail risk: reading VaR and CVaR
var.intro: A loss boundary and a tail average answer different questions. This fixed example using real SPY and AGG history illustrates the calculation only. {exampleLabel}.

s1.heading: The question behind tail risk
s1.p1: Tail risk asks roughly how much a bad day or month could cost, and how deep the worst days or months were on average. Value at Risk (VaR) marks a loss boundary at a chosen confidence level. Conditional Value at Risk (CVaR), also called Expected Shortfall, describes the average loss in that tail. Both measures here come from the same replay of today’s holdings. They describe a distribution of historical changes, rather than a forecast for the next day or month.
s1.p2: How to read it: at 95%, the example’s one-day VaR is {dayVar}. On about 95 of every 100 days in the replay the portfolio lost less than {dayVar}. On the other 5 days it lost more, and CVaR ({dayCvar}) is their average loss.

s2.heading: The daily-return distribution
s2.p1: Each bar counts days in a band of daily return. Losses are on the left and gains on the right; the bin width is 0.005. The example has {dailyCount} daily returns. The marked VaR and CVaR lines refer to the 95% one-day tail. The dotted line is a separate questionnaire reference, drawn from a hypothetical conservative answer. Bar heights describe frequency, while distance to the left describes depth of loss. A small bar far to the left can represent a rare but deep observation.

s3.heading: One day and one month
s3.p1: The table expresses losses as percentages, with example amounts on a hypothetical USD 100,000 portfolio. The SPY rows provide the same historical calculation for the comparison series, with percentages only. Each confidence level has its own reference values. The one-day and one-month columns come from different sets of returns, so a monthly number describes a complete trading-day window rather than a daily result repeated across a month.

s4.heading: VaR is not the largest possible loss
s4.p1: The 95% one-day VaR is {dayVar}, yet the worst observed day lost {worstLoss} on {worstDate}. The worst day is already deeper than the VaR boundary inside this example’s own history. VaR is therefore not the largest possible loss. It separates most observations from a smaller tail, leaving the size of losses in that tail open. Events absent from the window cannot be represented by its historical observations.

s5.heading: Why CVaR appears beside VaR
s5.p1: CVaR averages the losses in the selected tail; at 95% for one day it is {dayCvar}. The historical calculation sorts returns, takes the tail count rounded upward, and uses the loss at the boundary for VaR and the average of that tail for CVaR. The two appear together because a boundary alone does not describe the depth of the observations beyond it. Expected Shortfall is another name for this tail average, not a prediction of the next loss.

s6.heading: What confidence levels leave in the tail
s6.p1: At 95%, the daily tail has {dailyK95} observations. At 99%, it has just {dailyK99} out of {dailyCount}. The narrower tail rests on fewer observations even though both levels use the same history. A single deep day can therefore have more influence on its average. The product displays 99% only when there are at least 500 daily returns. That sample gate describes data availability, without judging a confidence level or the resulting loss.

s7.heading: Overlapping monthly windows
s7.p1: The one-month horizon uses actual overlapping returns across 21 trading days. Here there are {monthCount} windows, but only about {independentMonths} non-overlapping months. Adjacent windows share most of their days, so they are not independent samples. The tool does not multiply the daily figure by the square root of 21. That shortcut assumes independent, identically distributed days; the historical monthly calculation instead retains the changes observed across each full window.

s8.heading: Historical simulation and the normal model
s8.p1: Historical simulation uses the observed returns directly. The normal model fits a bell-shaped distribution to their mean and sample standard deviation. At 95%, the one-day VaR figures are close: {dayVar} historically and {normal95} under the normal model. At 99%, they differ: {dayVar99} and {normal99}. There were {fatCount} days below the mean minus three standard deviations, against {normalExpected} expected under a normal distribution. The table also compares CVaR. The product presents the normal model only as a one-line comparison inside calculation details.

s9.heading: What proxies can hide
s9.p1: An exchange-traded fund (ETF) tracks an index and combines many assets. When it represents a single holding without usable history, its path is usually smoother than that holding’s own path. The substituted history can consequently understate tail losses. The card shows a notice whenever any proxied share is positive. The example’s own SPY and AGG history illustrates the method; it does not remove this limitation for other holdings.

s10.heading: The questionnaire reference line
s10.p1: The reference starts with the Overview Risk ‘exceeds’ annualized-volatility threshold: 20%, 30% or 40% for conservative, balanced or aggressive answers. A short horizon or capital-preservation objective shifts it down by 5 percentage points, floored at 20%. It converts that volatility to a daily and monthly loss under a zero-mean normal assumption. Historical VaR uses the actual distribution, so the bases differ. The line is a comparison only, with no ‘within’ or ‘beyond’ judgement; what is acceptable differs by person and over time. It appears as a table row and a dotted daily-histogram line, and is absent when the questionnaire is unanswered.

s11.heading: Why there is no same-data backtest
s11.p1: Historical VaR is exceeded on about five percent of the days used to estimate its 95% boundary, by construction. Counting those same observations again adds no independent information about performance on new data. An out-of-sample rolling test would estimate from one window and measure subsequent observations. That test is not offered at present, so this guide does not present an in-sample exceedance count as validation.

s12.heading: The window limits the picture
s12.p1: The results describe only the five-year replay window and today’s holdings. Events outside that window are absent, and today’s collection brings hindsight into earlier dates. The measures do not describe every possible market event or your actual trading history. A historical tail is a summary of the observations available to this calculation, with the disclosed proxy and currency assumptions, rather than a complete account of future losses.

s13.heading: References
s13.p1: J.P. Morgan/Reuters, RiskMetrics — Technical Document (1996). Artzner, Delbaen, Eber & Heath, Coherent Measures of Risk, Mathematical Finance 9(3), 1999. Rockafellar & Uryasev, Optimization of Conditional Value-at-Risk, Journal of Risk 2(3), 2000. Acerbi & Tasche, On the Coherence of Expected Shortfall, Journal of Banking & Finance 26(7), 2002.

index.title: How Jade's portfolio tools work
index.intro: Jade's method explanations are public. Every guide uses a fixed example portfolio to illustrate a calculation, with real price history and readable tables beside the charts. {exampleLabel}. The examples describe past movement, without assessing a person's choices. Results computed from your own holdings are available with Jade. These six guides cover the Jade tools and the separate holdings rebalancing what-if page.

summaries.whatIf: A historical calculation of current holdings and up to two user-edited versions, with separate rebalancing rules.
summaries.replay: See how today's unchanged holdings are replayed through past prices, and what cumulative return, volatility and maximum drawdown measure.
summaries.var: Read historical loss distributions, the VaR boundary and the average loss beyond it, with their sampling limits.
summaries.stress: Follow a past market shock and see how each asset class contributed to the example's peak-to-trough return.
summaries.style: Understand the market styles that most closely resemble recent returns, and why fitted weights differ from actual holdings.

stress.title: Historical stress scenarios: reading the paths and contributions
stress.intro: This guide uses {portfolio} at the beginning of a historical window, with unchanged quantities afterwards. The example uses real price history and illustrates the method only. {exampleLabel}. The comparison line is SPY, an exchange-traded fund (ETF) that tracks the S&P 500. An ETF is a fund traded on an exchange; here it represents a broad market rather than an individual company's history.
stress.curveCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Peak {peak}, trough {trough}. Peak-to-trough return: {shock}, SPY {spyShock}. Largest drawdown: {drawdown}, SPY {spyDrawdown}. End of the peak-relative curves: {endReturn}, SPY {spyEndReturn}.
stress.barsCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Equity contribution {equityContribution} points; bond contribution {bondContribution} points; total {shock}. SPY represented {peakWeight} at the peak.
stress.tableCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Returns across the shock and the entire window.
stress.contributionCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Asset-class contributions to the peak-to-trough return.

s1.heading: What the tool answers
s1.p1: The tool asks how today's holdings would have moved through a past market shock. Each window begins with today's value weights, then lets prices change the mix without rebalancing it. This keeps the starting composition comparable across episodes. It does not reconstruct the transactions made at the time, or assume that today's holdings existed in your account then. The result is a replay of the past, not a forecast.

s2.heading: One episode, two curves
s2.p1: This example shows the 2025 tariff shock only. The Jade card offers all five episodes; the four other buttons here are greyed out and cannot be selected. Both curves use the same dates and have zero at the S&P 500 peak. The example's line and SPY's line describe different mixtures over the same market episode, so a gap between them reflects that difference in composition.

s3.heading: The shock in percentages and dollars
s3.p1: The example's peak-to-trough return is {shock}, compared with {spyShock} for SPY. Applied to USD 100,000, the example change is {amount}. That dollar figure gives the percentage a scale; it is not an account balance or a separate calculation of loss. The table also reports the largest drawdown across the entire window, alongside its own high and low dates. All figures describe this fixed example.

s4.heading: How the window is defined
s4.p1: A window runs from six months before the S&P 500 closing peak to six months after its closing trough. Here that is {start} to {end}. The dashed vertical line marks {peak}, and the dotted line marks {trough}. Zero on the chart means the value at the peak, not the value at the beginning of the window. Values before the peak can therefore be below zero even before the named shock begins.

s5.heading: Peak to trough and largest drawdown
s5.p1: Peak to trough fixes the dates using the S&P 500 episode. Largest drawdown searches for the deepest fall from any earlier high to a later low in the portfolio's own window. These are different questions. In this example both identify {peak} to {trough}, and the example's largest drawdown is {drawdown}. In other episodes, a portfolio concentrated in another market can reach its high or low on other days.

s6.heading: Reading the contribution bars
s6.p1: The contributions explain the total by asset class. They use each class's price change and its weight at the peak, rather than simply multiplying a loss by the starting weight. This matters because weights already drifted before the shock. The equity and bond contributions are {equityContribution} and {bondContribution} percentage points. Their sum equals the example's peak-to-trough return, apart from display rounding.
s6.r1: The center line is zero. A bar extending left pulled the portfolio down; one extending right added to its value.
s6.r2: A bar reflects both the asset class's movement and its share of the portfolio. SPY was {peakWeight} of the example at the peak.
s6.r3: Lengths are scaled to the largest absolute contribution. The longest bar fills half the track; a shorter bar is a fraction of that length, not an absolute percentage of the track.
s6.r4: The numbers add up to {shock}. The bond contribution partly offsets the equity contribution in this episode; the bars describe that arithmetic without rating either asset class.

s7.heading: Proxies and beta
s7.p1: A holding without its own history at the window start follows its replay proxy ETF until its own history begins. Beta is the estimated strength of its movement relative to that ETF, and scales the proxy's returns. An index proxy loses the holding's individual swings, so a scenario can understate its losses. The card states the approximated share and shows an amber note when that share is 66% or more. This example uses the two funds' own histories.

s8.heading: Earlier episodes and substitute history
s8.p1: The 2000–2002 and 2008 episodes reach back before some ETFs existed. A fixed substitute chain supplies the first available candidate with the required dates, using mutual funds or indexes. Some substitutes are price indexes that exclude dividends, rather than total-return series with dividends reinvested. Exchange rates before 2021-09 come from a one-time FRED export; FRED is the Federal Reserve Economic Data service. The amber note above the table appears for an approximated share of at least 66%, any substitute, or any price index.

s9.heading: What is not shown
s9.p1: There is no recovery metric. The curve after the trough shows the following six months, but that segment does not establish when a portfolio recovered its earlier high. There is also no questionnaire reference line. The historical paths and contributions answer what happened to a defined mixture through an episode; they do not compare a loss with a person's questionnaire answers.

s10.heading: Limits of five past episodes
s10.p1: Only five past episodes are represented. Other market events, including events unlike any of these, are absent. Today's holdings also carry hindsight: their presence today can reflect what became known later. Prices, proxies and substitute series set further limits on what the calculation describes. History does not repeat in the same form, and a fixed historical path supplies no probability for the next shock.

s11.heading: References
s11.p1: Basel Committee on Banking Supervision, Principles for Sound Stress Testing Practices and Supervision (2009).
s11.p2: Berkowitz, J., A Coherent Framework for Stress-Testing, Journal of Risk 2(2), 2000.

style.title: Style exposure: resemblance in returns
style.intro: The example begins as {portfolio} on {start} and keeps the quantities unchanged through {end}. It uses real price history to illustrate a returns-based calculation. {exampleLabel}. An exchange-traded fund (ETF) is a fund traded on an exchange. The ETFs below represent broad market styles, so their price histories provide a common language for comparing portfolios that contain different kinds of holdings.
style.barsCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Growth plus value {equityStyles}; aggregate bonds plus long-term Treasuries {bondStyles}; BIL {bilWeight}. R-squared {r2}, SPY {spyR2}; unexplained volatility {residualVol}, SPY {spyResidualVol}. Each style weight is repeated in the table.
style.curveCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Example cumulative return {cumulative}; style-mix cumulative return {mixCumulative}. The fitted mix uses {samples} overlapping three-day returns.
style.tableCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. Equivalent style weights and fit, with SPY for comparison.

s1.heading: What the tool answers
s1.p1: Style exposure asks which mix of broad market styles moved most like the portfolio over the last three months. The answer is a statistical resemblance, not a list of what is owned. Different holdings can move together because they respond to similar market forces. A fitted mix makes that shared movement visible, while the unexplained part records what the broad styles did not capture in this particular window.

s2.heading: Why use returns-based style analysis
s2.p1: Sharpe's returns-based style analysis compares sequences of returns, rather than scoring each stock's characteristics. Per-stock factor models need information about the underlying companies. Funds, wealth products and parts of Asian markets do not always have that information in a comparable form. Returns provide a shared observable series. The calculation finds non-negative weights that minimize the squared differences between the portfolio's returns and the style mix's returns, with a total weight of 100%.

s3.heading: The thirteen styles
s3.p1: The basis contains 13 styles, listed below with their ETF tickers. Growth, value and small-cap distinguish parts of the US stock market; other rows cover markets and asset classes outside it. Quality, low-volatility and momentum are omitted because their correlations with US large-cap exceed 0.9. Highly similar series make their individual weights difficult to distinguish. Long-term Treasuries, represented by TLT, remain separate from aggregate bonds because their interest-rate exposure differs. BIL represents cash and short-term bills in USD. REIT means real estate investment trust: a listed company owning income-producing property.

s4.heading: Reading the style bars
s4.p1: The table shows the fitted example beside a separate fit of SPY over the same dates. Each colored bar begins at the left edge and uses its own weight as a fraction of the cell width. Unlike the stress contribution chart, there is no central zero line and no scaling to the longest bar. The numbers and bar lengths express the same weights.
s4.r1: Weights are zero or more and add up to 100%. They describe an equivalent mixture under the stated constraints.
s4.r2: US large-cap growth plus value is {equityStyles}; aggregate bonds plus long-term Treasuries is {bondStyles}. These are close to the example's known starting stock and bond mix.
s4.r3: BIL receives {bilWeight} even though the example owns no T-bills. This is an equivalent exposure, not a holding discovered in the portfolio.
s4.r4: Weights of a few tenths of a percent in Hong Kong equities and real estate are statistical noise. Their presence does not establish an underlying position.
s4.r5: A row appears when either fitted weight is positive after rounding to six decimals. SPY therefore displays {zeroWeight} on the bond rows. Rows follow the basis order in this guide.

s5.heading: Comparing the two cumulative curves
s5.p1: The example returned {cumulative} over the window, while the style mix returned {mixCumulative}. The example line uses unchanged quantities. The fitted curve starts with the estimated weights and follows each basis ETF's cumulative price change, also without rebalancing. The solver fits overlapping returns; it does not force every cumulative point, or the last point, to match. A small gap in the cumulative chart is therefore compatible with a close statistical fit.

s6.heading: R-squared and unexplained volatility
s6.p1: R-squared (R²), the coefficient of determination, measures the fraction of return variation explained by the fitted styles. It is one minus the variance of the residuals divided by the variance of the example's returns. Residuals are the differences left after fitting. R² is displayed rounded down to two decimals: {r2} for the example and {spyR2} for SPY. Unexplained volatility is the residual standard deviation, annualized using the three-day horizon: {residualVol} and {spyResidualVol}. An amber note appears below 0.60; no low-fit example is shown here.

s7.heading: Three months and overlapping three-day returns
s7.p1: The fixed three-month window describes recent behavior, independently of the replay span. Markets close at different times, so a single day's Asian and US prices can reflect different information. Returns over overlapping 3-day intervals soften that misalignment. This example has {samples} returns from {levels} price levels. Neighboring intervals share days and are not independent observations. With fewer than 42 samples the card displays insufficient data, rather than a fitted mixture.

s8.heading: Constraints and uncertainty
s8.p1: The solver enforces non-negative weights and a total of 100%, and solves that constrained problem directly. It does not allow a negative weight to offset another style. No standard errors are supplied. The weights depend on the window and on the chosen basis, so a precise percentage is a numerical solution for these samples, not a statement that the exposure is known with that precision.

s9.heading: How proxies affect fit
s9.p1: A holding represented by a proxy already follows an index ETF. That ETF can itself closely resemble one of the basis styles, mechanically making the fitted result closer. The card displays a note whenever any proxied share is positive. A high fit can therefore partly reflect how the replay was constructed, rather than independent information about the original holding. Proxy disclosure remains relevant even when both cumulative curves look almost identical.

s10.heading: Boundaries of the analysis
s10.p1: The questionnaire is not used. There is no rolling drift view or per-holding breakdown. The result describes one recent historical window for the portfolio as a whole. It does not assign a judgement to a style, measure whether the mixture fits a person's circumstances, or forecast how these exposures behave in another window.

s11.heading: References
s11.p1: Sharpe, W. F., Asset Allocation: Management Style and Performance Measurement, Journal of Portfolio Management 18(2), 1992.
s11.p2: Fama & French, Common Risk Factors in the Returns on Stocks and Bonds, Journal of Financial Economics 33(1), 1993.
s11.p3: Carhart, M., On Persistence in Mutual Fund Performance, Journal of Finance 52(1), 1997.

tracking.title: Tracking error: the return gap and its variability
tracking.intro: This guide compares {portfolio}, with unchanged quantities, against two reference mixtures using real price history. {exampleLabel}. The references are a daily constant stock-and-bond mix and SPY alone. SPY and AGG are exchange-traded funds (ETFs), funds traded on an exchange, representing the S&P 500 and US aggregate bonds. The same example shows how both the choice of ingredients and rebalancing affect the comparison.
tracking.curveCaption: {portfolio}, {start} to {end}. {exampleLabel}. End excess against the daily constant mix: {balancedExcess} points; against SPY: {spyExcess} points. Mix minimum {balancedMin} on {balancedMinDate}, maximum {balancedMax} on {balancedMaxDate}; SPY minimum {spyMin} on {spyMinDate}, maximum {spyMax} on {spyMaxDate}.
tracking.tableCaption: {portfolio}. {reference}. {exampleLabel}. One-year window {oneStart} to {end}; five-year window {start} to {end}.

s1.heading: What the tool answers
s1.p1: Tracking asks how far, and how steadily, the holdings diverge from a reference you define. Excess return describes the gap between the two cumulative results; tracking error describes how much their return differences vary. The result describes that difference only. It does not judge whether the reference is appropriate for you or whether either portfolio's result meets a personal objective. These questions depend on information outside the calculation.

s2.heading: Defining a reference
s2.p1: A reference contains 1 to 5 components from 23 cached ETFs plus cash in the display currency. Whole percentages add up to 100%, and each user has one saved reference. When none is saved, the card uses 60% SPY + 40% AGG, marked as an example. The available funds represent markets and styles; cash keeps a constant value in the display currency. The reference editor defines the comparison mixture without changing the holdings used in the replay.

s3.heading: Daily constant weights versus unchanged quantities
s3.p1: The reference returns to its stated weights every day. Each day's return is the weighted sum of its components' returns, linked to the previous day's index value. The replay keeps quantities unchanged, so price movements change its weights. Even with identical ingredients and identical starting weights, these two rules create different paths. This comparison models those rules; it does not model trading costs or reconstruct transactions in an account.

s4.heading: Reading the five-year excess curves
s4.p1: The dashed horizontal line is zero: both sides have the same cumulative return there. Above it, the example's cumulative return is greater; below it, the reference's is greater. The curves end at {balancedExcess} percentage points against the daily constant mix and {spyExcess} against SPY. The caption also states each curve's minimum and maximum with dates. A curve's level is a cumulative gap, not a daily return or the tracking-error figure.

s5.heading: Comparing one year and five years
s5.p1: Each table uses a fresh starting mix at the beginning of its own window. The one-year and five-year columns therefore answer separate historical comparisons, rather than cutting the last year from an already-drifted five-year portfolio. The tables repeat the card's cumulative and annualized rows and tracking error, with {oneSamples} overlapping samples for one year and {fiveSamples} for five years. Amounts are percentages or percentage points, without a judgement label.

s6.heading: The same-assets comparison
s6.p1: Against the daily constant stock-and-bond mix, the ingredients are the same. The example is not rebalanced, and SPY's share drifted from 60% to {endWeight} over five years in a rising stock market. This explains its positive excess and its small but non-zero tracking error: {oneBalancedTe} over one year and {fiveBalancedTe} over five years. The difference comes from the paths created by the two weight rules, even though both portfolios began with the same funds.

s7.heading: The SPY comparison
s7.p1: SPY alone has different ingredients from the example. Tracking error is {oneSpyTe} over one year and {fiveSpyTe} over five years. Roughly, a 5% tracking error means the yearly gap typically varied by about 5 percentage points. It does not mean a fixed 5% loss, or specify which side finishes ahead. The final excess can be negative while tracking error remains positive, because a standard deviation measures variability without carrying the direction of the final gap.

s8.heading: Cumulative and annualized excess return
s8.p1: Cumulative excess is the example's cumulative return minus the reference's cumulative return, expressed in percentage points. Annualized excess subtracts their two separately annualized returns. It is not the annualization of the gap itself. Calendar days determine the annualization period. Short spans magnify this conversion, so an annualized difference can look large even when the underlying cumulative difference covers only a brief interval.

s9.heading: Why overlapping five-day returns
s9.p1: Tracking error uses the sample standard deviation of overlapping 5-day return differences, multiplied by the square root of 252/5. Markets close at different times; daily returns can reflect that timing rather than a difference in exposure. On Hong Kong and A-share mixtures, daily tracking error was 1.6 to 1.8 times the five-day figure; for US-only mixtures it was about 0.9 to 1.05 times. At least 10 samples are required. Overlapping windows share days and are not independent samples.

s10.heading: Window, currency and missing data
s10.p1: The comparison follows the replay span, from 1M to 5Y, with a 1Y default, and follows its display currency. Components use historical exchange rates on each date. If a component lacks data needed for the comparison, the reference is unavailable; another fund is not substituted. The example's tables illustrate the one-year and five-year spans only. Different windows can contain different events and produce different comparisons.

s11.heading: Why there is no information ratio
s11.p1: The information ratio is not offered. It evaluates active management and can become unstable on short spans. This tool describes a gap and its variability without turning that comparison into a judgement about management or personal fit. Like the other Jade tools, it records historical movement of today's mixture, rather than predicting a future result.

s12.heading: References
s12.p1: Roll, R., A Mean/Variance Analysis of Tracking Error, Journal of Portfolio Management 18(4), 1992.

agentGuide.title: Automate your holdings updates with your own agent
agentGuide.what: With active Jade, your own agent can turn an institution's holdings export into an updated current book in Portfonia. It checks the source, reads your book, prepares and validates changes, writes them, and checks change history. Your agent and tooling handle institution access, exports and scheduling. Portfonia does not log in to institutions, download statements or schedule these runs; it stores and updates your holdings records and does not execute trades.
agentGuide.how: On the AI Agent page, create a holdings-write token for an agent that updates holdings, or a read-only token for one that only reads. Give your agent the token and https://portfonia.com/llms.txt. It first calls GET /agent/v1/token (Verify token permissions). An updating agent stops if capabilities.holdings_write is false; a read-only agent stops if capabilities.holdings_read is false.
steps: Check that the source export covers every account at the institution and has the expected as-of date. Skip a partial or stale export.
Read GET /agent/v1/holdings and keep the returned version and each holding's id.
Match existing rows by stable holding ID, never by ticker alone. The same instrument in two accounts is two rows.

Change only rows belonging to this institution. Use POST /agent/v1/holdings to create, PATCH /agent/v1/holdings/{holding_id} to update, or DELETE /agent/v1/holdings/{holding_id} to delete. A single DELETE removes the ID in the path. Alternatively, PUT /agent/v1/holdings must list every other row unchanged: retain existing rows in holdings and explicitly list deleted IDs in delete_ids. An existing row omitted from both lists makes the whole request fail.

Before creation, whole replacement, single-row replacement or PATCH, call POST /agent/v1/holdings/validate with operation create, replace_all, replace or patch and the corresponding fields described in agent.md. Continue only if valid is true, then write using the current version. Single-row replacement uses PUT /agent/v1/holdings/{holding_id}. Deletion has no validation step; send its current version in the quoted If-Match header instead of a JSON body. Validation does not reserve a version or guarantee a later write.
On 409 version_conflict, read the book again and recompute the intended change. Never resend an old body with only its version swapped. Use the returned version for each subsequent write.

For POST creation, send an Idempotency-Key. After a timeout, retry with the same key and the same body, including the original version, within 24 hours to get the original result. Read again before another write.

Afterwards, read GET /agent/v1/holdings/changes with inclusive ET start and end dates within the last 30 days to confirm what changed. If truncated is true, narrow the date range. Unchanged writes and idempotent replays create no change-history group.
agentGuide.limits: Jade allows 100 stored holding rows, counting cash and watched rows. Single-row writes share 30 requests per minute and 100 per hour across your tokens. Reads, whole PUT and validation use the normal read limits. Quiet windows pause requests from five minutes before a heavy scheduled task until five minutes after it ends; use Retry-After when a request is refused. The last holding cannot be deleted through the API; clear the entire book only on the web. Successful current-holdings, change-history, snapshot and Jade risk-result reads share at most one access notice per ET day. Successful writes may trigger a separate daily modification notice; validation and idempotent replay send no data notice. A notice link revokes every token on your account at once, including other agents' tokens. It stops future access and does not undo saved changes. An Agent write or file upload that sharply reduces holdings rows or changes total value may trigger a separate alert email, at most one per Eastern Time date of the write.
agentGuide.effect: Writes update Portfonia's saved current book. Later briefings and the Jade tools—holdings replay, tail risk, historical stress scenarios, style exposure and tracking—use the updated book. Every request is audit-logged; the audit stores request metadata, not holding bodies or complete tokens.
